title: Section 1.9: Solving Linear Inequalities & Interval Notation
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 15 • Section 1.9 (Workbook p. 25)
detail: Lecture 15: Solving Linear Inequalities, Interval Notation & Unit 1 Grand Review
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### The Golden Rule of Inequalities (Workbook p. 25-26)
$$\text{When you MULTIPLY or DIVIDE both sides by a NEGATIVE number,}$$ $$\text{you MUST REVERSE (FLIP) the inequality symbol!}$$
- Example: $-2x < 6 \implies \frac{-2x}{-2} > \frac{6}{-2} \implies \mathbf{x > -3}$.
- **Interval Notation:** Parentheses $( \ )$ for strict ($<, >$), brackets $[ \ ]$ for inclusive ($\le, \ge$).
- **Infinities:** $\infty$ and $-\infty$ **ALWAYS take parentheses**.
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Strict: } & x > a \implies (a, \infty) \quad \text{and} \quad x < a \implies (-\infty, a) \\
\text{Inclusive: } & x \ge a \implies [a, \infty) \quad \text{and} \quad x \le a \implies (-\infty, a]
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Sora's Absolute Rule:** If you don't flip the sign when dividing by a negative, your entire solution set is reversed and wrong!
script:
[Prof. Park] Welcome everyone to Lecture 15 of M090 Introductory Algebra! I am Professor Eunju Park, and joining me at the teaching desk is TA Sora.

[TA Sora] Today is a celebration: we complete Section 1.9 on workbook pages 25 through 27: Solving Linear Inequalities, Graphing on Number Lines, and Interval Notationâand we conduct our Grand Unit 1 Review! Hello everyone!

[Prof. Park] Today we transition from equations (where two sides are equal) to INEQUALITIES (where one side is strictly greater than, less than, or equal to the other side). In real life, conditions are rarely exact equalities.

[TA Sora] When civil engineers design the bridge over the Gallatin River on Interstate 90, the load limit is an inequality: Weight â¤ 80,000 pounds. When backcountry skiers check avalanche danger at Bridger Bowl, snowpack temperature must stay below freezing: T < 32Â° Fahrenheit.

[Prof. Park] Today, we learn how to solve inequalities, express their infinite solution sets on number lines, and write them in standard INTERVAL NOTATION!

[TA Sora] And we must introduce the single most famous rule in all of inequality algebra: The Golden Rule of Inequalities: When you MULTIPLY or DIVIDE both sides of an inequality by a NEGATIVE number, you MUST REVERSE (FLIP) the inequality symbol!

[Prof. Park] If it was less than, it becomes greater than! If it was greater than or equal to, it becomes less than or equal to! Sora, explain why this flip happens with simple numbers. Look at 2 and 5. We all agree that 2 < 5.

[TA Sora] Now multiply both numbers by -1: 2 becomes -2, and 5 becomes -5. Which is larger: owing 2 dollars or owing 5 dollars? -2 is larger than -5! So -2 > -5! The symbol FLIPPED from less-than to greater-than!

[Prof. Park] Multiplying by a negative reflects the numbers across zero to the opposite side of the number line, reversing their relative order! Remember: only flip the symbol when you multiply or divide by a NEGATIVE number. Let's begin on slide 2!

[TA Sora] Let's reflect on the number line to understand why the inequality symbol flips: Imagine a giant mirror sitting right at the origin, zero: x = 0.

[Prof. Park] If you are standing at +3 and your friend is standing at +7, your friend is farther to the right: 3 < 7. Now reflect both of your positions across the mirror by multiplying by -1: You are now at -3, and your friend is at -7!

[TA Sora] On the negative side of the mirror, who is farther to the right? YOU ARE! -3 is closer to zero and farther right than -7! So -3 > -7!

[Prof. Park] Multiplying by a negative literally flips the entire universe of numbers across the mirror, turning right into left and left into right! That mirror analogy makes it impossible to forget! Whenever a negative number multiplies or divides across an inequality, the world flips!

title: Example 1A & 1B: Basic Interval Notation
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 15 • Section 1.9 Example 1A & 1B (Workbook p. 25)
detail: Lecture 15: Solving Linear Inequalities, Interval Notation & Unit 1 Grand Review
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Represent each on a number line graph and convert to interval notation (Workbook p. 25)
$$\text{A. } x > 5$$
$$\text{B. } x < -6$$
pitfall: **Order Matters:** In interval notation, always list numbers from LEFT to RIGHT as they appear on the number line! $(-\infty, -6)$, NOT $(-6, -\infty)$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 2 covers Section 1.9 Examples 1A and 1B from workbook page 25: Basic Interval Notation and Number Line Graphing: Part A: x > 5. Part B: x < -6.

[TA Sora] Let's master our notation conventions: Strict inequalities (< and >) use an OPEN circle on the graph and PARENTHESES ( ) in interval notation because the boundary endpoint is NOT included!

[Prof. Park] Inclusive inequalities (â¤ and â¥) use a CLOSED (solid) circle or square bracket [ ] because the boundary endpoint IS included! And infinity (â) and negative infinity (-â) ALWAYS take parentheses ( ) because infinity is a direction, not a reachable number!

[TA Sora] Now let's graph Part A: x > 5. On the number line, place an open parenthesis at 5 and shade everything to the RIGHT toward positive infinity. In interval notation, read from left to right: (5, â). Now look at Part B: x < -6.

[Prof. Park] Place an open parenthesis at -6 and shade everything to the LEFT toward negative infinity. Reading from left to right: (-â, -6). Always write the smaller (leftmost) number first in interval notation!

[TA Sora] Let's review interval notation formatting: Interval notation ALWAYS reads from left to rightâfrom smaller numbers to larger numbers! Never write (â, 5) or (-6, -â)! Negative infinity is the furthest possible destination to the left, so it must ALWAYS be on the left: (-â, -6).

[Prof. Park] Positive infinity is the furthest destination to the right, so it must ALWAYS be on the right: (5, â)!

title: Example 1C & 1D: Variable on the Right Side
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 15 • Section 1.9 Example 1C & 1D (Workbook p. 25)
detail: Lecture 15: Solving Linear Inequalities, Interval Notation & Unit 1 Grand Review
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Represent on number line and convert to interval notation (Workbook p. 25)
$$\text{C. } -3 \le x$$
$$\text{D. } 12 \ge x$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Part\ C:}\quad & \text{Step 1: Rewrite with } x \text{ on the left side (keep arrow pointing at } -3\text{):} \\
& -3 \le x \iff \mathbf{x \ge -3} \\
& \text{Solid bracket at } -3, \text{ shade right: } \mathbf{[-3, \infty)} \\[1em]
\mathbf{Part\ D:}\quad & \text{Step 1: Rewrite with } x \text{ on the left side (arrow points at } x\text{):} \\
& 12 \ge x \iff \mathbf{x \le 12} \\
& \text{Solid bracket at } 12, \text{ shade left: } \mathbf{(-\infty, 12]}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Reading Direction Trap:** When $x$ is on the right, read from the variable! $-3 \le x$ means '$x$ is greater than or equal to $-3$'! Always rewrite with $x$ on the left first!
script:
[Prof. Park] On slide 3, we look at Section 1.9 Examples 1C and 1D on workbook page 25: Inequalities with the variable on the RIGHT side: Part C: -3 â¤ x. Part D: 12 â¥ x. Danger alert!

[TA Sora] When the variable is on the right side, students often shade in the wrong direction! In Part C: -3 â¤ x.

[Prof. Park] Read it from the variable's perspective: 'x is GREATER THAN OR EQUAL TO -3!' If you flip the sides to put x on the left, remember that the inequality mouth stays open toward x: x â¥ -3!

[TA Sora] Now it is crystal clear: at -3, place a solid bracket [ and shade to the RIGHT! In interval notation: [-3, â)! Now look at Part D: 12 â¥ x.

[Prof. Park] Read it starting with x: 'x is LESS THAN OR EQUAL TO 12!' Rewriting with x on the left: x â¤ 12. On the number line, place a solid bracket ] at 12 and shade to the LEFT toward -â. In interval notation: (-â, 12]!

[TA Sora] Always rewrite inequalities with the variable on the left if you are ever unsure of the shading direction.

[Prof. Park] In Examples 1C and 1D, notice why reading from the variable's perspective is essential: When students read -3 â¤ x from left to right as 'negative 3 is less than or equal to x', they hear the words 'less than' and immediately want to shade to the left!

[TA Sora] That is a fatal trap! Always turn around and read starting with the variable: 'x is GREATER than or equal to -3!' The wide opening of the inequality symbol faces x, which means x is the larger quantity, pointing to the right!

title: Example 1E & 1F: Double (Bounded) Inequalities
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 15 • Section 1.9 Example 1E & 1F (Workbook p. 25)
detail: Lecture 15: Solving Linear Inequalities, Interval Notation & Unit 1 Grand Review
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Represent on number line and convert to interval notation (Workbook p. 25)
$$\text{E. } -3 < x < 1$$
$$\text{F. } 2 \le x < 3$$
pitfall: **Mixed Endpoints:** In 1F, $2$ is included (bracket $[$), but $3$ is strict (parenthesis $)$). Never write $[2, 3]$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 4 covers Section 1.9 Examples 1E and 1F on workbook page 25: Double (Bounded) Inequalities: Part E: -3 < x < 1. Part F: 2 â¤ x < 3. A double inequality describes a bounded interval sandwiched between two finite endpoints!

[TA Sora] In Part E: -3 < x < 1. x is simultaneously greater than -3 AND less than 1! On the number line, shade the region strictly BETWEEN -3 and 1. Since both symbols are strict (<), use parentheses on both ends: (-3, 1)!

[Prof. Park] Now look at Part F: 2 â¤ x < 3. Here, 2 is included (â¤), but 3 is excluded (<)! At 2, place a solid bracket [ . At 3, place an open parenthesis ) . Shade between 2 and 3. In interval notation: [2, 3)!

[TA Sora] This is called a half-open interval. In agricultural quality control, grain moisture content must often fall into bounded intervals like this to prevent spoilage during winter storage.

[Prof. Park] In agricultural applications across the Gallatin Valley, grain moisture content for winter wheat storage must be strictly between 12% and 14%: 12 < m < 14. If moisture exceeds 14%, grain molds and can spontaneously combust in grain elevators.

[TA Sora] If moisture drops below 12%, grain kernels crack during milling. Bounded intervals like (-3, 1) and [2, 3) define the safe operational zones in biology, chemistry, and manufacturing.

[Prof. Park] Remember our classroom motto: discipline with steps yields effortless accuracy on exams!

[Prof. Park] Exactly! Take it line by line, check each arithmetic move, and celebrate every victory!

title: Example 1G & 1H: Disjoint Compound Inequalities (Union)
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 15 • Section 1.9 Example 1G & 1H (Workbook p. 25)
detail: Lecture 15: Solving Linear Inequalities, Interval Notation & Unit 1 Grand Review
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Represent on number line and convert to interval notation (Workbook p. 25)
$$\text{G. } x < -7 \text{ or } x \ge 0$$
$$\text{H. } x \le 2 \text{ or } x > 5$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Part\ G:}\quad & \text{Two separate arrows pointing outward:} \\
& x < -7 \implies (-\infty, -7) \\
& x \ge 0 \implies [0, \infty) \\
& \text{Combine with union symbol } \cup: \mathbf{(-\infty, -7) \cup [0, \infty)} \\[1em]
\mathbf{Part\ H:}\quad & x \le 2 \implies (-\infty, 2] \\
& x > 5 \implies (5, \infty) \\
& \text{Combine with union: } \mathbf{(-\infty, 2] \cup (5, \infty)}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Union Symbol:** Use $\cup$ (union) to glue two disjoint intervals together!
script:
[Prof. Park] On slide 5, we examine Section 1.9 Examples 1G and 1H: Disjoint Compound Inequalities using the Union Symbol (âª): Part G: x < -7 or x â¥ 0. Part H: x â¤ 2 or x > 5.

[TA Sora] When you see the word 'OR', the solution set consists of two separate, non-overlapping intervals! In Part G: x < -7 OR x â¥ 0. First piece: x < -7 is (-â, -7). Second piece: x â¥ 0 is [0, â).

[Prof. Park] To combine them into a single mathematical statement, we use the UNION operator âª (which looks like a capital U): (-â, -7) âª [0, â)! Now look at Part H: x â¤ 2 or x > 5. Left piece: x â¤ 2 gives (-â, 2].

[TA Sora] Right piece: x > 5 gives (5, â). United together: (-â, 2] âª (5, â). The union symbol represents 'taking everything in either set.'
Notice the union symbol âª in compound inequalities: In computer programming and database querying (like SQL), âª represents the OR operator.

[Prof. Park] If a point belongs to either the left interval OR the right interval, it is accepted into the solution set! In contrast, the intersection symbol â© (an upside-down U) represents ANDâwhere intervals overlap.

title: Example 2A & 2B: Solving Linear Inequalities
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 15 • Section 1.9 Example 2A & 2B (Workbook p. 26)
detail: Lecture 15: Solving Linear Inequalities, Interval Notation & Unit 1 Grand Review
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Solve each inequality. Write final answer in interval notation (Workbook p. 26)
$$\text{A. } -6 + 3x \le -12 + 5x$$
$$\text{B. } 4(5x - 7) > 10 + 5x$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Part\ A:}\quad & 3x - 5x \le -12 + 6 \\
& -2x \le -6 \\
& \text{Divide by } -2 \text{ and } \textbf{FLIP the inequality sign!} \\
& x \ge \frac{-6}{-2} \implies x \ge 3 \implies \mathbf{[3, \infty)} \\[1em]
\mathbf{Part\ B:}\quad & 20x - 28 > 10 + 5x \\
& 20x - 5x > 10 + 28 \\
& 15x > 38 \\
& x > \frac{38}{15} \implies \mathbf{\left(\frac{38}{15}, \infty\right)}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **The Flip in 2A:** Dividing $-2x \le -6$ by $-2$ FLIPS the sign to $\ge$: $x \ge 3$, meaning $[3, \infty)$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 6 moves to Section 1.9 Examples 2A and 2B on workbook page 26: Solving Linear Inequalities algebraically: Part A: -6 + 3x â¤ -12 + 5x. Part B: 4(5x - 7) > 10 + 5x.

[TA Sora] Solving inequalities follows the exact same balance scale steps as solving equations, with one exception: watch out for dividing by a negative! Let's solve Part A: -6 + 3x â¤ -12 + 5x. Subtract 5x from both sides: -6 - 2x â¤ -12.

[Prof. Park] Add 6 to both sides: -2x â¤ -6. Now divide both sides by -2: DANGER! We are dividing by NEGATIVE 2! FLIP the symbol from â¤ to â¥! x â¥ (-6) / (-2) = 3! So x â¥ 3. In interval notation: [3, â)!

[TA Sora] Now let's solve Part B: 4(5x - 7) > 10 + 5x. Distribute the 4: 20x - 28 > 10 + 5x. Subtract 5x from both sides: 15x - 28 > 10. Add 28 to both sides: 15x > 38.

[Prof. Park] Divide by positive 15: since 15 is positive, do NOT flip the symbol! x > 38/15. In interval notation: (38/15, â)! In Example 2A: -6 + 3x â¤ -12 + 5x, what if a student subtracted 3x instead of 5x?

[TA Sora] Let's see: subtract 3x: -6 â¤ -12 + 2x. Add 12: 6 â¤ 2x. Divide by positive 2: 3 â¤ x! Reading from x: x â¥ 3!

[Prof. Park] Notice that by moving the variable to the right, the coefficient was positive (+2), so they never had to divide by a negative or flip the sign! Both algebraic paths lead to the exact same interval [3, â)!

title: Example 2C & 2D: Inequalities with Fractions & Negatives
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 15 • Section 1.9 Example 2C & 2D (Workbook p. 26)
detail: Lecture 15: Solving Linear Inequalities, Interval Notation & Unit 1 Grand Review
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Solve each inequality and write in interval notation (Workbook p. 26)
$$\text{C. } \frac{4}{5}y + 5 < 6$$
$$\text{D. } 2 \le \frac{x}{-8} - 3$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Part\ C:}\quad & \text{Subtract } 5: \quad \frac{4}{5}y < 1 \\
& \text{Multiply by } \frac{5}{4}: \quad y < \frac{5}{4} \implies \mathbf{\left(-\infty, \frac{5}{4}\right)} \\[1em]
\mathbf{Part\ D:}\quad & \text{Add } 3 \text{ to both sides:} \quad 5 \le \frac{x}{-8} \\
& \text{Multiply by } -8 \text{ and } \textbf{FLIP the inequality sign!} \\
& -8 \cdot 5 \ge x \implies -40 \ge x \iff x \le -40 \\
& \mathbf{(-\infty, -40]}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Multiplying by Negative Denominator:** In 2D, multiplying by $-8$ flips $\le$ to $\ge$! $-40 \ge x$ means $x \le -40$, which is $(-\infty, -40]$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 7 presents Section 1.9 Examples 2C and 2D on workbook page 26: Inequalities with Fractions and Negative Denominators: Part C: (4/5)y + 5 < 6. Part D: 2 â¤ x / (-8) - 3. In Part C: (4/5)y + 5 < 6.

[TA Sora] Subtract 5 from both sides: (4/5)y < 1. Multiply both sides by reciprocal 5/4: y < 5/4. In interval notation: (-â, 5/4)! Now look at Part D: 2 â¤ x / (-8) - 3. Add 3 to both sides: 5 â¤ x / (-8).

[Prof. Park] To clear the denominator, multiply both sides by -8! DANGER! Multiplying by -8 FLIPS the inequality symbol from â¤ to â¥! 5 Â· (-8) â¥ x, which gives: -40 â¥ x! Reading from x: x â¤ -40! In interval notation: (-â, -40]! That symbol flip was critical!

[TA Sora] In Example 2D: 2 â¤ x / (-8) - 3, notice how clearing the negative denominator flips the symbol: 5 â¤ x / (-8) multiplied by -8 gives -40 â¥ x, which is x â¤ -40!

[Prof. Park] Let's check with a number in the interval, say x = -48: Right side: -48 / -8 - 3 = 6 - 3 = 3. Is 2 â¤ 3? Yes, 2 is less than 3! The inequality holds true!

title: Example 2E & 2F: Binomial Numerator Inequality Comparison
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 15 • Section 1.9 Example 2E & 2F (Workbook p. 26)
detail: Lecture 15: Solving Linear Inequalities, Interval Notation & Unit 1 Grand Review
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Solve both and compare the effect of negative denominator (Workbook p. 26)
$$\text{E. } \frac{x - 30}{-4} \ge 50$$
$$\text{F. } \frac{x - 30}{4} > 50$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Part\ E:}\quad & \text{Multiply by } -4 \text{ and } \textbf{FLIP} \ge \text{ to } \le: \\
& x - 30 \le 50 \cdot (-4) \\
& x - 30 \le -200 \implies x \le -170 \implies \mathbf{(-\infty, -170]} \\[1em]
\mathbf{Part\ F:}\quad & \text{Multiply by positive } 4 \text{ (sign does } \textbf{NOT} \text{ flip!):} \\
& x - 30 > 50 \cdot 4 \\
& x - 30 > 200 \implies x > 230 \implies \mathbf{(230, \infty)}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Compare the Two:** In 2E, the $-4$ in the denominator flips $\ge$ to $\le$, pointing left! In 2F, the positive $4$ keeps $>$ pointing right! Two totally different answers!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 8 features Section 1.9 Examples 2E and 2F on workbook page 26: A side-by-side comparison of positive vs. negative denominators: Part E: (x - 30) / (-4) â¥ 50. Part F: (x - 30) / 4 > 50.

[TA Sora] Look at Part E: (x - 30) / (-4) â¥ 50. Multiply both sides by -4: this FLIPS the symbol from â¥ to â¤! x - 30 â¤ 50 Â· (-4) = -200. Add 30 to both sides: x â¤ -200 + 30 = -170!

[Prof. Park] Interval notation: (-â, -170]! Now look at Part F: (x - 30) / 4 > 50. Multiply both sides by +4: since 4 is positive, do NOT flip the symbol! x - 30 > 50 Â· 4 = 200. Add 30 to both sides: x > 230!

[TA Sora] Interval notation: (230, â)! Look at the dramatic difference: Part E yields numbers below -170, while Part F yields numbers above +230! That single negative sign completely inverted the entire solution domain!

[Prof. Park] Look at the visual contrast between Examples 2E and 2F: In 2E, dividing by -4 gives x â¤ -170: (-â, -170]. In 2F, dividing by +4 gives x > 230: (230, â). That comparison shows why attention to negative signs is the hallmark of a true mathematician.

title: Unit 1 Grand Review & Sora's 10 Core Commandments
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 15 • Unit 1 Complete Synthesis
detail: Lecture 15: Solving Linear Inequalities, Interval Notation & Unit 1 Grand Review
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Congratulations on Completing Unit 1 (Sections 1.0 - 1.9)!
- **1. Order of Operations:** PEMDAS always rules.
- **2. Substitution:** Always wrap substituted numbers in parentheses.
- **3. Exponents:** $a^0 = 1$, $a^{-n} = \frac{1}{a^n}$, $a^m a^n = a^{m+n}$, $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$.
- **4. Distributive Property:** Watch minus signs inside parentheses!
- **5. Polynomial Multiplication:** FOIL requires $(2y - 7)^2 = 4y^2 - 28y + 49$.
- **6. Rational Expressions:** Add/subtract ONLY with common denominator (LCD).
- **7. Linear Equations:** Balance scale—isolate the variable.
- **8. Equation Clearing:** Multiply EVERY term by LCD to clear fractions.
- **9. Classification:** Conditional (1 solution), Identity (all real numbers), Contradiction (no solution).
- **10. Inequalities:** FLIP the symbol when multiplying or dividing by a negative number!
solution: $$\mathbf{\text{Unit 1 Mastered! Next Up: Unit 2 — Graphing, Lines, and Functions!}}$$
pitfall: **Confidence Note:** Review all 15 workbook sections before Exam 1. You have every tool you need to succeed!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 9 concludes Lecture 15 and marks the completion of Unit 1! Let's celebrate everyone's incredible dedication across Sections 1.0 through 1.9 with Sora's 10 Core Commandments of Algebra! Here are our 10 Golden Commandments: 1.

[TA Sora] Order of Operations: PEMDAS always rulesâparentheses, exponents, multiply/divide left to right, add/subtract left to right! 2. Substitution: Always wrap substituted numbers in protective parentheses to preserve signs! 3. Exponents: Product rule adds powers, quotient rule subtracts powers, negative exponents take the elevator! 4.

[Prof. Park] Distributive Property: Watch minus signs in front of parenthesesâthey flip every sign inside! 5. Polynomial Multiplication: Binomial squared has a middle term! (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2! 6. Rational Expressions: Add and subtract ONLY over a common denominator! 7.

[TA Sora] Linear Equations: The balance scale ruleâisolate the variable using inverse operations! 8. Clearing Fractions: Multiply every term on both sides by the LCD to eliminate all fractions in one step! 9. Equation Classification: Conditional (one solution), Identity (all real numbers), Contradiction (no solution)! 10.

[Prof. Park] Inequalities: FLIP the inequality symbol whenever you multiply or divide by a negative number! With these 10 commandments etched into your algebraic toolbox, you are 100% prepared for Unit 2: Linear Equations in Two Variables and Graphing. Congratulations on conquering Unit 1 of M090 Introductory Algebra!

[TA Sora] As we close Unit 1, let's look at the incredible ground we have covered: From fractions, real numbers, and exponents in Sections 1.0 to 1.2, to polynomials and FOIL in Sections 1.3 and 1.4, to rational expressions in Section 1.5, and finally linear equations, clearing fractions, literal formulas, and inequalities in Sections 1.6 through 1.9!
